tasks.short: Follow trade magazines and online channels, attend courses and trade shows, and practise new styles and techniques.

steps.what: Barber follows trade magazines and online channels to stay informed of the latest styles
Barber attends courses and trade shows on hair care techniques
Barber practises new styles and techniques

tasks.design: Nothing changes. Following trends, attending courses and practising techniques are reading and hands-on learning that stay with the barber; there is no record or message to automate.
tasks.previous_blocker: Not applicable; the task has no paperwork.
tasks.still_hard: Trends move fast on social media.
tasks.human_edge: Judging which trend suits the salon's clients.

evidence.claim: Staying abreast of industry trends is reading that stays with the person.

assumptions: Boundary: from trend interest to the technique practised; using it on clients is outside.
Input contract: none; the task uses no data.
No new work: nothing changes in this task, so the added effort is zero.

incremental.description: No added work; nothing changes in this task.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: No saving in this task: following trends, attending courses and practising are reading and hands-on learning, and there is no record or message to take over.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Check stock on the shelves, look up products and prices with the wholesaler, decide quantities, place the order, and check the delivery and invoice.

steps.what: Barber checks stock of supplies on the shelves
Barber looks up products and prices in the wholesaler's webshop
Barber decides order quantities
Barber checks the final order in the webshop: products, quantities, prices and the delivery address
Barber orders supplies in the webshop
Barber checks the delivery against the order and the invoice that arrives in the accounting package
Barber checks the invoice before it is booked: supplier, lines and amounts against the delivery
Barber books the checked invoice in the accounting package

tasks.design: Retail stock in the salon system ({OPS_SYSTEM}) goes down with each sale at checkout, so the barber counts only professional products by hand. A saved reorder list in the wholesaler's webshop holds the usual products, so they are not looked up each time. The barber decides quantities, checks the order and places it. Invoices come into the accounting package ({ERP}) through the feed instead of being typed; the barber checks each against the delivery and books it.
tasks.previous_blocker: Stock was counted by eye and products looked up for every order.
tasks.enabler_now: Salon systems track retail stock; wholesalers' webshops keep reorder lists.
tasks.still_hard: Professional products used per client are not scanned.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing a busy holiday week needs extra stock.

evidence.claim: Salonized offers payments and a financial overview in its salon software.
The business keeps its administration, bills and receipts for seven years.

assumptions: Boundary: from stock low to the delivery checked; choosing a wholesaler is outside.
Input contract: retail products in the salon system; fallback is counting.

Ordering decisions and the checks before ordering and booking keep their full time. s1 keeps 50 because only professional products are counted by hand; s2 keeps 60 because the reorder list holds the usual products; s4 keeps 60 for placing the order; s5 keeps 60 because invoices are no longer typed.
research_questions: Do stock-outs of retail products fall?

incremental.description: Barber enters new retail products in the salon system.

approvals.approved_version: The order with products, quantities and prices exactly as checked by the barber in s4c, placed once in the wholesaler's webshop for delivery to the salon; any change needs a new check.
The wholesaler's invoice with lines and amounts exactly as checked by the barber in s5c, booked once in {ERP} against that delivery; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: mostly professional products that are counted by hand and invoices that still come on paper, so s1 and s5 keep 80 (23.7); high: mostly retail products and invoices through the feed (34.8).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Examine hair and scalp, ask about history and earlier treatments, suggest a treatment, and note the advice on the client card.

steps.what: Client gives consent for scalp notes in a short form at the first visit
Barber examines hair and scalp
Barber asks about history and earlier treatments
Barber suggests treatments to alleviate hair problems
Barber notes the advice on the paper client card

tasks.design: The digital client card in the salon system ({OPS_SYSTEM}) shows earlier treatments, products bought and notes, so the barber does not rely on the client remembering. Advice is noted on the card in a short field. Scalp conditions are noted only with the client's explicit consent. Examining and suggesting treatments stay with the barber.
tasks.previous_blocker: Earlier treatments were on paper cards or in the client's memory.
tasks.enabler_now: Salon systems hold digital client cards with history.
tasks.still_hard: Some scalp problems need a doctor, not a product.
tasks.human_edge: Recognising when to send a client to a doctor.

reach.learn: Whether advice builds on earlier visits.

evidence.claim: Salonized client cards hold treatment and purchase history, notes and before-and-after photos.
Notes on skin conditions or allergies are health data; outside a treatment contract this usually needs explicit consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from the client visit to advice noted; medical treatment is outside.
Input contract: client cards kept current; fallback is asking the client.
Examining and advising do not change.

Clients give consent in a short form at their first visit (s0c, client time); the barber records it (new work). s2 keeps 70 because the card shows earlier treatments and products instead of asking for all of them.
s4 is the barber's first note of the advice and keeps its full time.
unknowns: Clients with hair problems per week.
research_questions: Do repeat clients get advice that builds on earlier visits?

incremental.description: Barber records client consent for health notes.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: mostly new clients without history on the card, so s2 keeps 90 (1.5); high: regular clients with history (5.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Recommend lotions, tonics and other products, check stock, ring up the sale, and note purchases on the client card.

steps.what: Barber recommends lotions, tonics or other cosmetic supplies
Barber checks whether the product is in stock
Barber sells the product and takes payment
Barber notes purchases on the paper client card today; after the change selects the client at checkout so the sale goes on their card

tasks.design: Checkout in the salon system ({OPS_SYSTEM}) shows stock for each product and is linked to the card terminal, so the barber does not walk to the shelf or key in amounts twice. The sale is written to the client card at checkout, replacing the paper card note. Recommending products stays with the barber.
tasks.previous_blocker: Stock was checked on the shelf and purchases written on paper cards.
tasks.enabler_now: Salon checkouts show stock and write sales to client cards.
tasks.still_hard: Clients often decide to buy later.
tasks.human_edge: Recommending only what the client will really use.

reach.learn: Whether repeat purchases are easier to suggest.

evidence.claim: Salonized client cards hold treatment and purchase history.

assumptions: Boundary: from the client visit to the purchase noted; restocking is outside.
Input contract: products in the salon system; fallback is paper cards.

s4 copies the sale onto the card today; after the change checkout writes the sale to the card, so s4 keeps 20 for selecting the client at checkout. s3 keeps 70 because the terminal takes the amount from checkout while scanning and payment stay.
research_questions: Do product sales per client rise?

incremental.description: Barber corrects stock after damaged products.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: few product sales and stock often wrong in the system, so the barber still walks to the shelf; s2 keeps 80 and s3 keeps 85 (7.7); high: many sales per day with current stock (13.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The barber keeps cutting, advising, recommending and learning; stock counting, product look-ups and paper client cards shrink.
role.ambitious_version: A barber with more time in the chair.
